coverage: This release shows the conventional Big Five mass extinctions, placed on the ICS chart. Empty stretches are not periods where nothing happened. Lanes fill as their evidence is checked.

claims.label: Approximate extinction interval
claims.text: The review reports that most authorities place the extinction at about 445–443 million years ago.

source.citation: Harper DAT (2024) Late Ordovician Mass Extinction: Earth, fire and ice. National Science Review 11(1): nwad319
source.status: No correction, retraction or expression of concern on the publisher's page (checked 10 Nov 2026)

claims.label: Context
claims.text: The same section sets out three readings of how it unfolded: two main extinction pulses (the first at the base of the Hirnantian Stage, the second in its middle), a single more prolonged phase, or an additional earlier phase in the early Katian. The pulses are placed by rock layers, not by dates, so they are not drawn on the axis.

source.citation: Harper DAT (2024) Late Ordovician Mass Extinction: Earth, fire and ice. National Science Review 11(1): nwad319
source.status: No correction, retraction or expression of concern on the publisher's page (checked 10 Nov 2026)

entries.title: Frasnian–Famennian extinction (Late Devonian)
entries.scope: This entry covers the Frasnian–Famennian event only. The later end-Devonian (Hangenberg) crisis is outside this check.

claims.label: Boundary age: no older than
claims.text: A volcanic ash bed just below the Frasnian–Famennian boundary in Germany was dated to 372.360 ± 0.053 million years (2σ, measurement uncertainty only), so the boundary can be no older than 372.4 million years.

source.citation: Percival LME et al. (2018) Precisely dating the Frasnian–Famennian boundary: implications for the cause of the Late Devonian mass extinction. Scientific Reports 8: 9578
source.status: No correction, retraction or expression of concern on the publisher's page (checked 10 Nov 2026)

claims.label: Modelled boundary-age range
claims.text: Combining that date with a published age model gives a boundary age of 371.93–371.78 million years (371.86 ± 0.08).

source.citation: Percival LME et al. (2018) Precisely dating the Frasnian–Famennian boundary: implications for the cause of the Late Devonian mass extinction. Scientific Reports 8: 9578
source.status: No correction, retraction or expression of concern on the publisher's page (checked 10 Nov 2026)

assumptions: the cited age model is correct
sedimentation was constant between the two Kellwasser horizons

claims.label: Context
claims.text: These values date the boundary, not the length of the extinction. How long the extinction lasted is not shown.

claims.text: The authors place the onset of the mass extinction at 251.941 ± 0.037 million years ago, citing their earlier high-precision dating.

claims.label: Approximate age of the extinction horizon
claims.text: In all three sections studied, a large sulfur-isotope shift at about 201.5 million years ago coincides with the extinction horizon.

source.citation: He T et al. (2020) An enormous sulfur isotope excursion indicates marine anoxia during the end-Triassic mass extinction. Science Advances 6: eabb6704
source.status: No correction, retraction or expression of concern in the article text on the publisher's page (checked 10 Nov 2026)

claims.label: Context
claims.text: Other recent papers give slightly different round figures for the extinction: about 201.3 and 201.5 million years (both in one 2024 paper) and about 201 million years (2025).

source.citation: Bos R et al. (2024) Climate-forced Hg-remobilization associated with fern mutagenesis in the aftermath of the end-Triassic extinction. Nature Communications

claims.text: The extinction is placed at the dated impact because high-precision dating has established that the impact and the extinction were synchronous.
